title: Ship Agents that Ship: A Hands-On Workshop - Kyle Penfound, Jeremy Adams, Dagger
talk_summary: Dagger engineers demo building a coding agent where the agent's tools are typed Dagger functions (read/write/list files, a fixed test function) running in sandboxed containers, with the LLM plugged in as a component and the whole thing triggered from GitHub issues via Actions. The core message is that reliability comes from giving agents a narrow, typed, pre-defined tool surface plus a mandatory validation tool, and from full tracing of every tool call.

takeaways.technique: Narrow typed tool surface instead of shell access
takeaways.what_they_do: The agent gets only read_file, write_file, list_files and a single pre-defined test function; it cannot run arbitrary commands. Tool schemas are auto-generated from typed function signatures rather than hand-written JSON.
takeaways.evidence_quote: giving flexibility where it's important for completing tasks and removing it where you know exactly how things are meant to happen

takeaways.technique: Mandatory validation tool + post-agent re-run of tests
takeaways.what_they_do: Prompt tells the agent to always run the test tool and not stop until tests pass, and after the agent returns, the harness independently re-runs the same test function on the output before accepting it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: now run the test because this is all the same code that we're using throughout our project to run tests

takeaways.technique: Deterministic guardrail checks layered under LLM review
takeaways.what_they_do: They frame CI checks as guardrails that enforce standards the generative step can't be trusted to self-enforce, run outside the agent so the agent can't skip or edit them.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we need to enforce certain standards, right? It could be compliance things, could be like you say linting

takeaways.technique: Detect agents editing tests to make them pass
takeaways.what_they_do: They flag that agents will modify tests to get green, and suggest prompting or validation to detect test-file changes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: sometimes if the agent broke the test, it'll go change the test and sometimes that's correct

takeaways.technique: Compose agents as functions; wrap, don't rewrite
takeaways.what_they_do: The GitHub-issue agent is not a new agent — it reads the issue, calls the existing develop agent, then opens a PR. Agents can also be placed inside another agent's environment as a callable tool.

Each agent run edits files inside its own container sandbox and returns a new immutable directory object; the host filesystem is untouched until explicitly exported, so many agents can run concurrently.
takeaways.evidence_quote: They all have their own sandboxed workspace where they're editing these files. They're not messing up your local state
